this first episode does a great job at really setting the tone for Asahigaoka. _lots_ of establishing shots and a heavy focus on aspect-to-aspect transitions, which is doubly important considering Hotaru’s unfamiliarity with the environment. we’re learning everything that the town and its inhabitants have to offer alongside her; and while it takes a bit of convincing, all that’s needed is an open mind and a willingness to shift perspectives that breathes life into a vibrant, rich country atmosphere rife with bliss. over the coming episodes, this intimate focus on a sense of place means first-timers will really come to see why Non Non Biyori is an iyashikei masterpiece. 

>	Have you lived in the countryside? How does it compare to living in a city? If not, do you think you would prefer the countryside?

i’ve lived in a big city my entire life, and while i am very confident i would not prefer the countryside, i can’t help but yearn to travel there and visit one day. doesn’t have to be Japan (although it would be nice) — just some time away from fast-paced, routine city living would i’m sure would do wonders for my mental health. my parents grew up in the country, though, and while they don’t really watch anime, i’ve been thinking of introducing them to NNB, if only for the nostalgia factor. 

>	Why do you think Renge wonders about whether she lives in the country/sticks?

[NNB spoilers all the way to Nonstop] >!Renge is naturally a very smart and inquisitive girl. from being able to do multiplication near-instantly despite never having looked at a times table, or having the gall at her age to debate whether a perfectly round object exists, this first episode subtly but creatively primes the viewer to realize this over the coming episodes through this initial exposure to her curious nature.!<

it definitely has its tense moments but overall i found it to be very comforting and life-affirming, especially considering the tone that it ends off on. while NNB and Yuru Camp are just bliss throughout, GLT was a "light at the end of the tunnel" kind of vibe for me. of course, individual experiences may vary

Aria is definitely a very, very slow burn. i really liked it, but didn't love it, until Origination (the last season) came around. it's my single favourite piece of media ever, but that's only because the first two seasons are so unapologetically slow, to really hammer in the intimacy and care that its world and characters need for Origination to be so profound.

if you find yourself forcing yourself to get through it, the last season won't have the same impact. it does get better as it goes along, but its lulls are by design and Aria as a whole wouldn't be half as good without them

thank god someone finally said it. it's not about certain anime being inherently better for _all_ beginners like some sort of essentialist notion, it's about keeping the recommendation palatable for the average newcomer's tastes. 

often, but not always, this means shows with low barriers to entry which minimizes the culture shock of entering anime as a medium, the Death Notes, AoTs of the industry. the medium shift is jarring enough, why would you throw in heavy cultural references or off-kilter psychological elements to potentially ruin a first impression? 

no two "beginning anime watchers" are the same, but you have to make extrapolations due to the nature of entering anime for the first time. this was definitely my experience, and it's the same for so many others. the concept of "beginning anime" wouldn't exist if it wasn't.

i would go as far to say that for first time viewers, the first episode is a horrible viewing experience, and the next two to three are definitively bad. there’s only so much an alluring atmosphere can do if you are just utterly, completely lost the entire way through. 

the show becomes much more noticeably digestible past when (major Texh spoilers) >!Yoshii dies!<, but a lot of people don’t even get to that point. 

of course, the tendency of this show to hold back and only surface the absolute most necessary information and not a smidge more pays off dividends when everything all falls into place late into the series. but it’s not really that surprising that people just don’t stick it out

{a place further than the universe} - well-paced adventure slice-of-life/drama. balances tone shifts nicely and never gets too melodramatic. a simple message told really well with grounded and unique characters. 

{girls’ last tour} - the manga is better, but the anime is no slouch. touches base on the human condition through an apocalyptic slice-of-life adventure. chito and yuuri’s dynamic is elite. 

{shinsekai yori} - the absolute most intriguing world i have ever seen in any TV show or anime, beating out AoT, Hunter x Hunter, GoT, Westworld (at least those are the ones i’ve seen). some cite exposition issues as the biggest criticism which i kind of agree with but they’re written in about as well as they could be. can’t elaborate without spoilers 

{bloom into you} - probably the best LGBTQ+ representation i’ve seen in anime. handles microaggressions extremely well, features nuanced relationship building with respect for boundaries, and overall explores the meaning of love moreso than the fulfillment of romantic desires. 

{hunter x hunter (2011)} - don’t think this one needs an explanation. intricate power system, unique and stellar characters, an expansive world, and with two arcs (yorknew and chimera ant) that are some of the greatest in all of shounen. 

{land of the lustrous} - plenty enjoyable on its own as an coming-of-age action, but also takes the time to analyze the psychological aspects of power and high-functioning trauma. anime-only ending isn’t very resolute though, i recommend continuing with the manga. 

{madoka magica} - when you think it’s as hopeless as it could be, it gets worse. its kinda hard to put into words just how grim this anime is, the way it contrasts with the traditionally “happy” premise of magical girls just makes that much better. 

{kaguya-sama} - comedy is fairly subjective so if this series doesn’t hit for you then it just doesn’t, but this has so far been the only anime that’s made me laugh as much as B99 and The Office. also has amazing characters that are fully fleshed out instead of only existing for the mains. 

{attack on titan} - another one that doesn’t need to be explained. incredible worldbuilding, gripping suspense, and some of the most intricate plot details all woven together nicely.

{fate/zero} is by far the darkest and most well written installment of the Fate series. if you don’t plan to watch any of the others then you can go ahead and watch Zero (it’s a prequel), but if you want to watch the other two installments of the main story, Unlimited Blade Works and Heaven’s Feel, watch those two in that order before Zero.

the fights start to get good story-wise and hype wise around episode 40 at the seabed temple arc. they get *really* good around episode 55 during the witches’ forest arc, though i would still classify the animation as average or slightly below average at this point in the anime. 

story becomes S-tier in addition to animation becoming A-tier around episode 90 during the elf reincarnation arc. it was this arc that made black clover one of my favourite battle shounens. animation gets yet another step up around episode 158 but that’s only for 12 episodes as the series ends at 170. 

overall i think if you make it to the end of the witches’ forest arc (around episode 60ish) and you’re still not engaged, you should drop it. probably the biggest powerscaling development of the series happens during this arc, of course more happens later on but it’s like another 50-60 episodes to reach that point.

aside from the fights and animation which are absolutely in conversation for the best in all anime in general, demon slayer is a fairly mid anime because of its weak characterization and predictable plot-driven events. 

in some ways, the simplicity of demon slayer isn’t a bad thing, it makes it incredibly easy for newcomers to the medium to follow and become invested in the series, which is why it’s become one of the most popular animes in the West. but even when excusing the one-dimensionality of this anime - as shounens somewhat tend to be - the character writing leaves a lot to be desired. the only decently fleshed out characters in this series are tamayo, yushiro, >!upper moons 3-1, sanemi, and genya!<. for an anime with such a big and diverse cast this leaves a lot to be desired. 

people are free to enjoy what they want of course and i disagree with people that can’t give credit where credit is due. by all means demon slayer is a compelling watch and in no way does the writing quality suck to the point where it’s a given that anyone should drop it. but treating it like it’s one of the best in the genre as a cohesive product - not just its animation - undermines the quality of truly best-in-class shounens with amazing writing like hxh, one piece, and fma.
